purpose: Quality eval for the research loop as the engine for ALL Ask (briefs/research-loop-contract.md). Thirteen questions: seven ordinary qualitative shapes and six multi-hop shapes. Graded structurally by scripts/research_eval_grade.mjs; the markdown report puts old and new answers side by side for the Fable judge.

gold.note: The 34-question agentic gold set is included with --set gold or --set all. Its rows are graded by scripts/agentic_ask_score.mjs (deterministic, record-computed expectations) plus the generic grounding checks below.

tools.note: expected_tools is the ideal order. The loop may choose differently; the harness reports the trail against it (subsequence = pass, all present in another order = partial) but does not fold it into the grade.

usefulness.pass: Answered (no refusal or decline) and every part of the question is covered by a fact or a cited source.
usefulness.partial: Answered, but at least one part of the question has no fact or source behind it.
usefulness.fail: Refused, declined, empty, or no part covered.

citations.pass: At least one cited source; every citation key resolves to a cited source; every sentence with a figure carries a citation; every quotation of 30+ characters and 6+ words is found verbatim in the evidence.
citations.partial: At least one cited source, but a figure sentence lacks a citation or a quotation cannot be found in the 600-character source window (ordinary payloads only carry windows).
citations.fail: No cited source, a citation key that resolves to nothing, or (when the evidence is complete fact text) a quotation that is not in the evidence.

correctness.pass: Every must check passes; no figure or roster name in the answer is absent from the facts and sources; no causal donation wording.
correctness.partial: At least half of the must checks pass and nothing is invented, or a figure or name is missing only from a windowed snippet in a cited sentence.
correctness.fail: An invented figure or name (absent from complete fact evidence, or in an uncited sentence), causal wording, or fewer than half of the must checks.

rubric.overall: fail if any axis fails; pass if all three pass; otherwise partial.

must_not.why: The model never writes figures: every number and amount must appear in the facts or cited sources.
No politician may be named unless a fact, cited source or the question names them.
No causation wording beside donations, votes or speeches.
A refusal or decline is a usefulness fail unless the question expects one.

questions.question: Which party's senators spoke most about housing since 2022, and how did they vote on the HAFF bill?

must.why: party rows with exact counts, and at least one count rendered
the leading party is named
a division or bill record for the HAFF bill is in the facts
a vote tally for the leading party, rendered in the answer
the period is inferred from the question, never chosen by the model
the federal Hansard gap mid-2022 to mid-2025 must be stated

rubric.usefulness: pass: names the leading party with its Senate housing count and that party's recorded votes on HAFF divisions; partial: ranking only (the one-shot planner's ceiling) or votes only; fail: refusal or neither part.
rubric.citations: pass: every count and tally cites a count link or division record; partial: a tally sentence lacks a citation; fail: no citations.
rubric.correctness: pass: counts and tallies match the facts, period since 2022, coverage caveat present; fail: any figure or party absent from the facts, or a vote attributed to a party the facts do not cover.

questions.question: How has the number of gambling speeches changed each year since 2015, and who led it?

must.why: one row per year from the trend tool
at least eight of the twelve years are rendered
a speaker row with an exact count, rendered
the leading speaker is a roster name bound to a fact
the window crosses the federal gap

rubric.usefulness: pass: a year-by-year series since 2015 and the leading speaker with a count; partial: the series without a leader (the planner's usual result) or a leader without the series; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: year rows and the leader cite reproducible count links; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: every year figure and the leader's count match the facts, no invented peak or percentage; fail: a figure not in the facts.

questions.question: Compare how often Labor and the Greens spoke about climate change in the Senate since 2022, and who was each party's most frequent speaker.

must.why: both parties named
a count for each party, rendered
a leading senator for each party, bound to a fact

rubric.usefulness: pass: both party counts and a leading senator for each; partial: party counts only; fail: refusal or one party missing.
rubric.citations: pass: every count cites a count link; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: counts match the facts and both named entities keep their own count (planRetainsNamedScope); fail: a party dropped from a count, or an invented name.

questions.question: How did Jacqui Lambie vote on gambling divisions, and what has she said about gambling in the Senate?

must.why: a vote tally from the divisions record, rendered
at least one cited Lambie speech

rubric.usefulness: pass: a recorded-vote tally and cited speech evidence; partial: speeches only (today's ordinary Ask cannot read divisions) or votes only; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: the tally cites division records and every quotation is verbatim in a cited speech; partial: a quotation outside the snippet window; fail: no citations or an invented quotation.
rubric.correctness: pass: tally figures match the facts, speeches attributed to Lambie only; fail: a vote figure not in the facts or a position attributed without a source.

questions.question: Which donors gave the most to the Nationals, and how many speeches about agriculture have Nationals MPs made since 2022?

must.why: disclosed donor rows with amounts, one rendered
the Nationals' agriculture count, rendered

rubric.usefulness: pass: named donors with amounts and the speech count; partial: one of the two; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: donor rows cite return references or the party money page, the count cites a count link; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: amounts and count match the facts, donors spelt as disclosed, no causal wording; fail: an amount not in the facts, a donor not in the facts, or any suggestion the money bought the speeches.

questions.question: Which Greens senator spoke most about gambling since 2022, and how did they vote on the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026?

must.why: a speaker row with an exact count, rendered
the leading senator is a roster name bound to a fact
that senator's tally on divisions titled with the bill, rendered

rubric.usefulness: pass: the leading Greens senator with a count and their aye/no tally on the bill's divisions; partial: ranking only; fail: refusal or a non-Greens leader.
rubric.citations: pass: count link and division records cited; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: the count and tally match the facts, the vote belongs to the same senator the ranking named; fail: a tally for a different person or an invented figure.

questions.question: What has Andrew Wilkie said about poker machine reform?

must.why: at least two cited Wilkie speeches

rubric.usefulness: pass: a grounded account of his positions with at least two cited speeches; partial: one speech or a vague summary; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: every quotation verbatim in a cited passage, claims cited; partial: a quotation outside the window; fail: none or invented.
rubric.correctness: pass: nothing attributed that the cited passages do not say, no figures beyond the passages; fail: an invented figure, date or name.

questions.question: How has Penny Wong's position on recognising a Palestinian state changed over time?

must.why: at least two cited Wong records
cited records at least two years apart

rubric.usefulness: pass: an evidenced sequence of what she said, dated, across at least two years; partial: a single-period position; fail: refusal or the evidence-gap reply when the record holds speeches.
rubric.citations: pass: each dated statement cites a Wong record and quotations are verbatim; partial: a quotation outside the window; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: dates and statements match the cited records, the position verifiers accept it; fail: a statement attributed without a record or a change asserted the records do not show.

questions.question: How do Labor and the Coalition differ on nuclear power?

must.why: cited speeches from at least two speakers
cited speakers from both sides (soft: unknown when the sources carry no speaker)

rubric.usefulness: pass: each side's position with cited speeches from that side; partial: one side evidenced; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: claims cited to speeches by the party they describe; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: positions match what the cited speakers said, party labels correct; fail: a position attributed to the wrong party or an invented name.

questions.question: What did David Pocock say about the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026?

must.why: a cited 2026 Pocock speech

rubric.usefulness: pass: what he argued on the bill with a cited 2026 speech; partial: general gambling remarks from other years; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: quotations verbatim in cited 2026 speeches; partial: outside the window; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: statements match the cited speech; fail: an invented amendment, vote or figure.

questions.question: How has Barnaby Joyce talked about climate change over the years?

must.why: cited records at least three years apart

rubric.usefulness: pass: a dated account across several years with cited speeches; partial: one period; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: each dated statement cites a Joyce speech, quotations verbatim; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: nothing beyond the cited speeches; fail: invented figures or statements.

questions.question: How do the Greens and One Nation differ on immigration?

rubric.usefulness: pass: each party's position with cited speeches from its own members; partial: one side; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: claims cited to the party's speakers; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: positions match the cited speeches; fail: a position attributed to the wrong party or an invented name.

questions.question: What arguments have been made in the Senate for and against a ban on gambling advertising?

must.why: at least two speakers cited

rubric.usefulness: pass: arguments on both sides, each cited to a Senate speaker; partial: one side; fail: refusal.
rubric.citations: pass: every argument cited, quotations verbatim; fail: none.
rubric.correctness: pass: arguments match the cited speeches and are attributed to the right speakers; fail: invented speakers or figures.

rubric.citations: Every amount and the coverage caveat has its source.
rubric.correctness: Tool-computed federal AEC published-selection totals; no personal payments or influence inference.
